steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on how language distance relates to the impact of fine-tuning on the representation spaces of multilingual language models, and how that connects to cross-lingual transfer.

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Language models have been shown to encode linguistic knowledge implicitly. For multilingual language models (MLLMs), previous research has also looked extensively at how these linguistic features influence cross-lingual transfer performance. But not much attention has been paid to how these factors affect the language representation spaces of MLLMs.

State-of-the-art MLLMs such as mBERT and XLM-R use a shared vocabulary and are meant to project text from any language into an embedding space that is language-agnostic. Even so, there is empirical evidence that these models encode language-specific information across all of their layers. This means that it may be possible to identify separate monolingual representation spaces inside the shared multilingual representation space.

- Our focus
  - past work: cross-linguality during fine-tuning, alignment of representation spaces of language pairs
  - ours: absolute impact on each language's representation space individually, not relative to another language
  - isolating per-language impact -> deeper study of inner modifications during fine-tuning
  - main objective: role of linguistic features here (known to affect transfer performance)
  - concretely: impact on target language representation space after fine-tuning on a source language vs. five language distance metrics
  - findings: relationships across all layers; stronger correlations in deeper layers; significant differences between distance metrics
- Inter-correlation
  - between language distance, impact on representation space, and transfer performance
  - hypothesis that may help cross-lingual transfer to linguistically distant languages
  - preliminary evidence that further investigation is merited

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Language models have been shown to encode linguistic knowledge implicitly. For multilingual language models (MLLMs), previous research has also looked extensively at how these linguistic features influence cross-lingual transfer performance. But not much attention has been paid to how these factors affect the language representation spaces of MLLMs.

State-of-the-art MLLMs such as mBERT and XLM-R use a shared vocabulary and are meant to project text from any language into an embedding space that is language-agnostic. Even so, there is empirical evidence that these models encode language-specific information across all of their layers. This means that it may be possible to identify separate monolingual representation spaces inside the shared multilingual representation space.

Past research focused on the cross-linguality of MLLMs during fine-tuning, and looked specifically at how the representation spaces of different language pairs are aligned. We instead focus on the absolute impact on the representation space of each language on its own, and not on the relative impact on one language's representation space compared to another language. If we isolate the impact for each language we can study in more depth the inner modifications that happen inside MLLMs during fine-tuning. The main objective of our study is to look at the role of linguistic features in this setting, because previous research showed that they have an impact on cross-lingual transfer performance. More specifically, we look at the relationship between the impact on the representation space of a target language after fine-tuning on a source language and five different language distance metrics. We observed such relationships in all layers, with a trend of stronger correlations in the deeper layers of the MLLM, and with significant differences between the language distance metrics.

We also observe an inter-correlation between language distance, impact on the representation space and transfer performance. Based on this we propose a hypothesis that may help to improve cross-lingual transfer to languages that are linguistically distant, and we give preliminary evidence that suggests our hypothesis is worth investigating further.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
It has been shown that language models implicitly encode linguistic knowledge [1,2]. For multilingual language models (MLLMs), previous research has also extensively investigated the influence of these linguistic features on cross-lingual transfer performance [3,4,5]. However, little attention has been paid to the impact of these factors on the language representation spaces of MLLMs.

Although state-of-the-art MLLMs such as mBERT [6] and XLM-R [7] use a shared vocabulary and are intended to project text from any language into a language-agnostic embedding space, empirical evidence shows that these models encode language-specific information across all layers [8,9]. This opens up the possibility of identifying distinct monolingual representation spaces within the shared multilingual representation space [10].

Past research has focused on the cross-linguality of MLLMs during fine-tuning, specifically on the alignment of the representation spaces of different language pairs [11,12]. Our focus, instead, is on the absolute impact on the representation space of each language individually, rather than the relative impact on the representation space of one language compared to another. Isolating the impact for each language allows a more in-depth study of the inner modifications that occur within MLLMs during fine-tuning. The main objective of our study is to examine the role of linguistic features in this context, since previous research has shown their impact on cross-lingual transfer performance. More specifically, we examine the relationship between the impact on the representation space of a target language after fine-tuning on a source language and five different language distance metrics. We observe such relationships across all layers, with a trend of stronger correlations in the deeper layers of the MLLM and significant differences between the language distance metrics.

Additionally, we observe an inter-correlation among language distance, impact on the representation space and transfer performance. Based on this observation, we propose a hypothesis that may help enhance cross-lingual transfer to linguistically distant languages, and we provide preliminary evidence suggesting that further investigation of this hypothesis is merited.
